newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-HINGIS IN A LEAGUE OF HER OWN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HINGIS IN A LEAGUE OF HER OWN.

text.p: The biggest complaint about women's tennis used to be that the sport was being dominated by a handful of players.
But all that's changed this year. Now it's being dominated by just one and the chances of Martina Hingis loosening her grip look increasingly remote.

In the space of six months, the 16-year-old Swiss teenager has turned the women's circuit into a monopoly, romping through the first half the season without a loss, stringing together 37 successive victories.
The only woman in Open era history to have started a year better is Steffi Graf, who still leads the way with her 45 successive wins in 1987.
Hingis, who took over the world number one ranking from Graf in March, has been collecting titles -- six this year -- like other teenagers her age hoard compact discs.
A 38th win on Saturday over Iva Majoli in the final of the French Open will give her a second consecutive grand slam title to go along with the Australian Open crown she lifted in January.

Tennis record books are full of teenage phenomena but the accomplishments of Hingis still stand out: the youngest player in the Open era to win a grand slam title, the youngest player to hold the number one world ranking, youngest player to reach $1 million in career earnings -- just a few of the firsts in a list which seems to grow with each match she plays.

Another footnote could be added on Saturday: victory in the French final would make her the youngest player in history to collect two grand slam titles, a record held since 1888 by Charlotte "Lottie" Dodd.
Many of the other records Hingis is rewriting belong to the player she beat to reach the final -- Monica Seles.

Seles was barely two months younger than Hingis is now when she won the first of her three French titles at Roland Garros in 1990. But she has now faced the irrepressible Swiss four times and lost on each occasion.

"Only time will tell if this is the Martina Hingis era," said Seles, who in 14 previous grand slam semifinal appearances had lost only once. "But the way Martina is playing is amazing, not just this tournament but throughout the year.
"She's tough mentally, she's very quick, she's just good everywhere. She has a great attitude and she's enjoying herself out there."
Clearly the main focus for Seles and the rest of the women's tour will be to find a way to keep Hingis from having so much fun.
But that will be more easily said than done against the fearless Swiss who has shown the steely nerve of an undercover operative and seems to revel in the Centre Court spotlight.
At the moment, there appears to be no stopping Hingis, on or off the court.

Just before the start of the French, Hingis was sidelined for six weeks when she was thrown from her horse and underwent arthroscopic surgery on her left knee. But she arrived in Paris showing few ill-effects.
So dominant has Hingis's performance been this season that even Seles, still feeling her way back after her stabbing in 1993, may have to start re-evaluating her future in the game.
"I don't think I would have come back after all that stuff if I really thought I'd be happy just getting to the quarter-finals and semifinals of grand slams," Seles admitted.
